title: Addresses and pointers
objectives: Read and write through a pointer, and see when one dangles.
Walk a range with a pair of pointers.

screens.title: A variable that holds an address
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You read `*p = 500` as changing `p`. The `*` means the `int` that `p` points at, which is `qty`.
Printing `qty` prints its value. Its address would be `&qty`.
`*p = 500` is the normal way to write through a pointer, so it compiles.

hints.text: What does the `*` in `*p = 500` refer to: the pointer, or what it points at?
Follow the dashed arrow from `p`'s box.
`*p` is the `int` at the address `p` holds, which is `qty`. Writing 500 there changes `qty`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the arrow: which box does `*p` reach?

byKey.three: You read `*p = 500` as changing `p`. The `*` reaches the `int` that `p` points at, which is `qty`.

explain.text: `p` holds `qty`'s address, so `*p` reaches `qty` itself. Writing 500 through `*p` changes `qty`. `p`'s own box still holds 0x1000.

screens.title: A pointer into a vector
screens.question: Tap the price that `*(p + 2)` reads.

hints.text: Where does `p` start?
`p` starts at index 1.
`p + 2` is two elements on from index 1, which is index 3. `*` reads the price there.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from where `p` points, not from the front.

byKey.c2: That is `*(p + 1)`. Move two elements from `px[1]`.
byKey.c1: That is `*p` itself. `p + 2` moves two elements on.
byKey.c0: `p` starts at `px[1]`, not `px[0]`. Count two on from there.

explain.text: `p` points at `px[1]`, so `p + 2` points at `px[3]`, and `*(p + 2)` reads 102.00. Pointer arithmetic counts whole elements, not bytes.

screens.title: Addresses move in steps of the type
screens.prose: `&x` is the **address of** `x`. `double* p` is a **pointer**: a variable holding an address. `*p` **dereferences** it, reaching the object there. The elements of `px` sit side by side, 8 bytes apart.
screens.question: How many bytes past `p`'s address is the address `p + 2` holds?

widget.label: Bytes past p
widget.accept: 16 bytes: 2 elements of 8 bytes each, so 0x1008 + 16 = 0x1018.

hints.text: `p + 2` moves two elements. How big is one element?
`px[1]` and `px[3]` are two steps apart on the line.
Each `double` is 8 bytes, so two elements are 16 bytes: 0x1008 + 16 = 0x1018.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the elements moved by the size of one `double`.

byKey.two: You counted elements. The address moves by 2 elements times 8 bytes.
byKey.twentyfour: That is the distance from `px[0]`. Measure from `p`, which starts at `px[1]`.

explain.text: `p + 2` moves two whole `double`s, and each is 8 bytes, so the address grows by 16: from 0x1008 to 0x1018. The compiler scales by `sizeof(double)` for you.

screens.title: Write through a pointer
screens.prose: `nullptr` is the pointer that points at nothing. Reading or writing through it is **undefined behaviour**: a desk build usually dies with `Segmentation fault`. Check for it first.
screens.question: Write `void bump(int* p)`: add 1 to the `int` that `p` points at, and do nothing when `p` is `nullptr`.

widget.postlude:
// reads the int at address 0, to see whether a call wrote through a null pointer
int null_word() { return *(volatile int*)0; }
widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 5 hidden tests. The last passes `nullptr` and checks that nothing was written. This browser build does not crash on a null write, so the test reads address 0 itself.

hints.text: Two steps: guard against `nullptr`, then write through `p`.
`*p += 1;` changes the `int` that `p` points at. `p += 1` would move the pointer instead.
`if (p == nullptr) return;` then `*p += 1;`.

feedback.correct: Guard, then write through the pointer.
feedback.generic: Not yet. The results under the editor say which test failed.

byKey.test-5: The `nullptr` test failed: the code wrote through a null pointer. Return before `*p` when `p == nullptr`.

explain.text: `*p += 1` changes the `int` at the address `p` holds, so the caller's `fills` becomes 8. The guard matters: a desk build would crash on `*p` with `p` null. This browser build quietly writes to address 0 instead, which is worse.

screens.title: Walk a pointer pair
screens.prose: A range can be passed as two pointers: `begin` at the first element, and `end` one *past* the last. `end` is never read. A hidden `max_of(v)` calls your function with `v.data()` and `v.data() + v.size()`.

state.caption: `end` points one past the last price

screens.question: Write `max_via_pointer(begin, end)`: the largest value in the range. An empty range (`begin == end`) returns 0.

tests.setup:
std::vector<double> v(100000);
for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) v[i] = (i * 37) % 1000;

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests, including all-negative prices and an empty range. One range sits mid-array, and nothing outside `begin` to `end` may be read.

hints.text: Start the best value at `*begin`, not at 0: prices can be negative returns.
A loop `for (const double* p = begin; p != end; ++p)` visits each element once.
Return 0 if `begin == end`. Otherwise set `best = *begin`, then for each `p` after it, keep `*p` if it is larger.

feedback.correct: `p != end` stops exactly at the last element.
feedback.generic: Not yet. The results under the editor say which test failed.

byKey.test-2: All three values are negative, so a best that starts at 0 never changes. Start from `*begin`.
byKey.test-5: The range is `xs[1]` to `xs[2]`. Read from `begin` and stop before `end`.

explain.text: `++p` moves one `double` on, and `p != end` stops before the address one past the last. Starting `best` at `*begin` handles negative values. This pair of pointers is exactly what `v.begin()` and `v.end()` generalise.

screens.title: It printed the right number
screens.question: Is the program correct?

options.text: No: `bid` ended at `}`, so `*p` reads a dead object, which is undefined behaviour
Yes: it printed the right price
options.why: That is the trap. The read is undefined: it may print the old value, a stray number or crash. The browser build happened to leave 101.25 there.
A pointer only holds an address. It does not keep the object alive; `bid` ends at its closing brace.
It compiles cleanly. The compiler cannot always see that `p` outlives `bid`.

hints.text: When does `bid` stop existing?
`bid` is declared inside `{ }`. Its life ends at the `}`.
After the `}`, `p` holds the address of a dead `double`. Reading it is undefined, whatever it prints.

feedback.correct: A right answer from undefined behaviour is luck.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether `bid` still exists when `*p` runs.

byKey.fine: That is the trap. The read is undefined; the browser build just left 101.25 in that memory. A desk build with checks stops here.
byKey.alive: A pointer does not keep its target alive. `bid` ended at its closing brace.

explain.text: `bid` ends at the inner `}`, and `p` is left **dangling**. Undefined behaviour means the compiler may do anything: this browser build is forgiving and printed the stale 101.25. A desk build with AddressSanitizer stops at that line, as the next screen shows.

The frame lists its objects; one of them is where the read landed.
`[32, 40) 'bid' (line 5)` is the 8 bytes of `bid`, declared on line 5, and the arrow says the read was inside it.

screens.title: Pointers in six lines
screens.prose:
What you used, in one place:

```cpp
int* p = &x;       // p holds x's address
*p = 5;            // write x through p
p = nullptr;       // points at nothing: never use *p
double* q = &px[0];
*(q + 2)           // px[2]: q + 2 moves 2 * 8 bytes
p == r             // same address? not same value
```

A pointer to a pointer, `int** pp = &p;`, holds the address of a pointer.
screens.question: `double a = 5.0, b = 5.0;` What does `std::cout << (&a == &b);` print?

options.why: You compared the values. `&a == &b` compares addresses, and two variables never share one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does `==` compare when both sides are addresses?

explain.text: `&a` and `&b` are two different addresses, so they compare unequal and `std::cout` prints 0 for `false`. To compare values through pointers, write `*p == *r`.

screens.title: Evaluate *(p + 2)
screens.prose: `px` starts at 0x1000, with 8-byte `double`s, and `p = &px[1]`. Each line below gives one step and its reason.
screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: 0x1018 = 0x1000 + 3 × 8, so it is the address of `px[3]`

hints.text: Start with what `p` holds.
Add before you dereference.
Address of `p`, then the address `p + 2`, then which element sits there, then read it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need an address before you can move it, and you move it before you read.

explain.text: `p` starts at 0x1008. Moving 2 elements adds 16 bytes, giving 0x1018, which is `px[3]`'s address. Only then does `*` read the value, 102.00, so `*(p + 2)` is `p[2]`.

screens.title: A C feed hands you pointers
screens.question: Which loop sums every level's size?

options.text: `for (const Level* p = levels; p != levels + n; ++p) total += p->size;`
`for (const Level* p = levels; p <= levels + n; ++p) total += p->size;`
options.why: `<=` also reads `levels + n`, one past the last level: memory the SDK never gave you.
`levels` never moves, so this adds the first level's size `n` times.

options.text: `for (const Level* p = levels; p != levels + n; p += sizeof(Level)) total += p->size;`
options.why: `++p` already moves one whole `Level`. Adding `sizeof(Level)`, 16, jumps 16 levels at a time: it skips most levels and can step over `levels + n`.

hints.text: Which pointer moves, by how much, and where must it stop?
`levels + n` is one past the last level, like `end`.
Start at `levels`, step with `++p`, stop when `p == levels + n`. Read `p->size` each time.

feedback.correct: One past the end, never read.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check where each loop starts, how it steps, and where it stops.

byKey.bytes: Pointer arithmetic already scales by the size of `Level`. Adding `sizeof(Level)` jumps 16 levels at a time.

explain.text: `++p` moves one `Level` (16 bytes), and `p != levels + n` stops before the address one past the last. Off-by-one reads like `<=` are undefined: a desk build may read the next object in memory, and nothing warns you.

ideas: `&x` is `x`'s address; a pointer `T* p` holds one, and `*p` reaches the object there. `p + k` moves `k` whole elements, `k * sizeof(T)` bytes.
`nullptr` points at nothing. Reading through it, or through a pointer to an object that has ended, is undefined behaviour.

This browser build is forgiving: null reads and dangling reads often print stale numbers. A desk build usually crashes on a null read. A dangling read may print a stale number there too; `-fsanitize=address` names the line.

formula.name: Pointer arithmetic
formula.note: A range is `[begin, end)`: `end` points one past the last element and is never read.

summary.trap: A program that prints the right number can still read a dead object. Undefined behaviour is not a crash you can rely on.

options.text: Undefined behaviour: a desk build usually stops with `Segmentation fault`
It prints 0, the value of a null pointer
options.why: `*p` reads the `int` at address 0, not the pointer's value. On a desk machine that page is not readable at all.
It compiles. The compiler does not track which pointers are null.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does `*p` read when `p` points at nothing?

explain.text: On Linux, g++'s build dies with `Segmentation fault` (AddressSanitizer: "SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000"). In this browser, address 0 is ordinary memory, so the read returns whatever `int` sits there; a test run with this app's compiler printed 0. Neither is a promise: guard with `if (p)`.

quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: `**pp` follows two arrows: `pp` to `p`, then `p` to `x`. Writing 7 there changes `x`.
`int** pp = &p;` is a pointer to a pointer. It compiles.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow `pp`, then follow what you find.

explain.text: `pp` holds `p`'s address, so `*pp` is `p`, and `**pp` is what `p` points at: `x`. Writing 7 through it changes `x`.

quiz.question: What does the compiler do with this function?

options.text: It compiles with a warning; the returned pointer dangles

options.why: clang only warns: "address of stack memory associated with local variable 'x' returned". The build still succeeds.

options.text: It compiles silently, and the pointer is safe
options.why: `x` ends when the function returns, so the caller gets the address of a dead object.

feedback.correct: A warning, not an error: read your warnings.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. When does `x` stop existing?

explain.text: `x` lives in `best_bid`'s frame and ends at its `}`. clang warns "address of stack memory associated with local variable 'x' returned", but builds anyway. Return the `double` itself instead.

quiz.question: An `int` is 4 bytes. `int* p` holds 0x2000. What address does `p + 3` hold?

options.why: You added 3 bytes. `p + 3` moves 3 whole `int`s: 3 × 4 = 12 bytes, which is 0xC.
You used 8 bytes per element, the size of a `double`. An `int` here is 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply 3 by the size of an `int`.

explain.text: Pointer arithmetic scales by the type: `p + 3` moves 3 × 4 = 12 bytes. 12 is C in hex, so the address is 0x200C.
